newsitem.title: CHINA: China says tariffs down to 15 percent by 2000.
newsitem.headline: China says tariffs down to 15 percent by 2000.

text.p: China, eager to win free trade kudos and speed its entry into the World Trade Organisation, on Monday vowed to cut tariffs to an average 15 percent by 2000 -- but diplomats said the promise signalled little policy change.

Beijing had made great efforts to promote the liberalisation of international trade and investment and planned to continue cutting import duties, the official Xinhua news agency quoted Chinese President Jiang Zemin as saying.

"China will bring it (the average tariff) further down to around 15 percent by the year 2000," Jiang said in an address to regional leaders at the Asian-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum at Subic Bay in the Philippines.

In the same speech, Jiang said it would be very difficult to liberalise trade in information technology according to a fixed timetable, suggesting Chinese reservations over a U.S.-led push for a global pact on free trade in such technology by 2000.

Jiang's speech came just a year after he stole the show at an APEC meeting in Japan with high-profile promises of tariff cuts, but Beijing-based diplomats said the Chinese president's latest vow was unlikely to repeat earlier success.
"This isn't of the same order," said a diplomat from an APEC member nation, adding that although the 2000 deadline for duty cuts appeared new, the target itself was already familiar.

China was eager to speed progress toward its long-cherished goal of membership in the World Trade Organisation (WTO), but the 15 percent tariff target alone would add little impetus to Beijing's campaign, the diplomat said.
"The 15 percent is nothing new," he said. "They have said for some time that's the target they are working to."

While the atmosphere at WTO negotiations had improved in recent months, the diplomats said much still needed to be done to hammer out the details of China's entry, which Beijing argues should be on the favourable terms accorded developing nations.

The United States and other WTO members argue that China's fast-expanding financial muscle means it should accept more exacting entry requirements, prompting Chinese accusations that Western forces are trying to stifle its economic growth.
Any cut in China's tariffs was a move in the right direction, but there was still a long way to go to WTO membership, a European diplomat said.
"From our perspective, 15 percent is not enough," he said. "China is well aware that they haven't done the deal with this announcement."
At last year's APEC meeting in the Japanese city of Osaka, Jiang upstaged fellow Asia-Pacific leaders by announcing plans to cut the tariffs guarding China's market by nearly one third.

The APEC announcement was backed up in April when Beijing slashed tariffs to an average 23 percent, a move welcomed by Chinese exporters but opposed by struggling state companies wary of increased foreign competition.
Chinese Premier Li Peng later said China would take vigorous steps to lower tariffs to 15 percent, a level he described as average for developing nations, but gave no timetable.

In a joint statement at the Subic Bay APEC meeting on Monday, APEC leaders called for an agreement by the WTO to substantially eliminate tariffs on information technology by 2000, but Jiang's speech suggested Chinese reservations.
Flexibility would be needed on the kind of products to be included in any liberalisation and efforts would be needed to eliminate barriers to technology transfer, Jiang said.

"However, because of the differences in the levels of economic development in the member economies, it is very difficult for the liberalisation in this field to be pushed forward in accordance with a timetable," he said.
